newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks gain on spillover buying.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks gain on spillover buying.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks rose Wednesday on spillover buying from the previous session's rally, but analysts said they were unsure whether the market had reached a bottom or if there was more downside ahead.
At 1 p.m. EDT, the Dow Jones industrial average was up 18.46 points at 6,605.62 after racing up 135 points Tuesday in its second biggest one-day gain ever.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances by a small margin on New York Stock Exchange volume of 261 million shares.
"The question is whether this is a dead-cat bounce, just a knee-jerk response after selling reached a peak," said Alfred Goldman, technical analyst at A.G. Edwards & Sons.
The Dow recovered smartly this week, erasing more than a quarter of the nearly 700-point drop posted after setting its last record high close of 7,085.16 on March 11.

"Have we seen our lows or is this just a lift?" Goldman asked. "The big picture is that we are still in a bull market, but on a short-term basis, meaning the next few days, we could still retest our lows."
He said he did not think the market had reached a bottom yet.

"We did not have the preconditions that exist at important bottoms. We did not have the anguish and panic dumping you normally see," Goldman said. "I still think it's a bull market, but I will let the market action of the next few days tell me whether we have seen 'the' turn or just 'a' turn."
The bond market fell after a strong data in the March industrial production and capacity utilization report revived inflation talk.
The 30-year Treasury bond was off more than a quarter point, sending its yield up to 7.12 percent from Tuesday's close of 7.07 percent. The price and yield move in opposite directions.
Industrial production rose 0.9 percent, compared with a revised 0.6 percent increase in February. Capacity utilization rose to 84.1 percent from a revised 83.6 in February.
Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp. said that the stock and bond markets mostly managed to get past the worrying data.
"The number that was particularly troubling was the capacity utilization figure because it suggested that the economy was operating at near full capacity," he said.

"That certainly stirred concerns that we would get upward pressure on prices," Johnson said. "The reason we got past that hurdle is because many people would argue that we are not measuring capacity utilization correctly, and that there is more excess capacity than currently shows up in the numbers."
He said that even if capacity were as high as the numbers indicated it was, "it is hard to get higher inflation when oil prices are declining and the dollar is strong."

The Dow got most of its impetus from a rally in Philip Morris Cos., which rose 2-7/8 to 41-3/4 on its first-quarter earnings. The gain also was spurred by news the U.S. tobacco industry has begun talks aimed at settling current lawsuits.
Eastman Kodak Co. was up 3-1/8 at 78-1/2 after reporting earnings on Tuesday that exceeded analysts' expectations.
Other tobacco shares also rallied, with RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. up 3-1/4 at 33-1/2, and Loews Corp., which owns Lorillard Tobacco Co., up 41-1/2 at 90-7/8.
Clarify Inc. slumped 9-3/4 to 7 after the company said it expected little, if any, revenue growth in the second quarter over the first.
The Nasdaq Composite index was off 5.15 points at 1,207.73.
